Active Fire Calendar: A Harmonized Fire History for Haut-Katanga, DR Congo

Satellites have monitored active fires for over 20 years using MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). However, differences in their resolution and sensitivity make their hotspot counts difficult to compare, limiting access to a consistent long-term fire record.

Our project aims to harmonize NASA FIRMS data from both sensors into a unified monthly time series and present it through an interactive web application featuring a fire calendar. Users can explore fire activity by area, identify the most active months and years, compare current activity with historical patterns, and export data as CSV.

Our case study focuses on Haut-Katanga, DR Congo, particularly its miombo savanna ecosystems, where seasonal fires are common. The tool supports researchers and emergency managers in understanding fire patterns and detecting possible changes in fire seasons.

The application and data pipeline are operational, currently using simulated demonstration data. MODIS-VIIRS calibration and integration of real satellite observations are the next development milestones.

The project is open source and built with Python, pandas, Streamlit and Plotly.
details:
Active Fire Calendar: A Harmonized Fire History for Haut-Katanga, DR Congo

Project Overview

Active Fire Calendar is an open-source project designed to improve the monitoring and understanding of fire activity through satellite observations. It addresses the challenge of combining historical fire data from two NASA satellite instruments: MODIS, which has provided observations since 2000, and VIIRS, which has been collecting data since 2012.

Although both instruments detect active fires and thermal anomalies, differences in spatial resolution and detection sensitivity make their observations difficult to compare directly. These inconsistencies can affect long-term analyses and make it challenging to identify reliable trends in fire activity.

Our project aims to harmonize NASA FIRMS active fire hotspot data from MODIS and VIIRS into a consistent monthly historical dataset. This unified record will provide a more coherent perspective on fire activity over time.

Our Solution

We are developing an interactive web application centered on a visual feature called the Fire Calendar. It organizes fire activity by month and year, using a color-coded system to highlight variations in hotspot activity.

Users can select a geographical area and explore historical fire patterns, identify the most active months and years, compare current monthly activity with historical median values, and investigate potential changes in seasonal fire patterns.

The platform also provides geographical hotspot visualization and allows users to export monthly time series and hotspot records in CSV format for further analysis.

Study Area and Environmental Relevance

Our initial case study focuses on Haut-Katanga Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, particularly the miombo savanna and woodland ecosystems.

This region experiences distinct seasonal fire patterns. Understanding when and where fire activity occurs can support environmental research, ecosystem monitoring, and informed decision-making by researchers and emergency management stakeholders.

The project focuses on identifying temporal and geographical patterns rather than assuming the causes of detected fires. Potential drivers, including agricultural burning and charcoal production, are treated as hypotheses requiring additional investigation.

Technology and Data Sources

The project uses NASA FIRMS as its primary source of active fire hotspot observations.

The development stack includes:

  • Python for data processing and analysis.
  • Pandas for data management and harmonization.
  • Streamlit for the interactive web application.
  • Plotly for dynamic charts and visualizations.

Current Development Status

The web application and data download pipeline are operational. The current application runs on simulated demonstration data while the MODIS-VIIRS calibration and integration of real satellite observations remain the next major development milestone.

The project is designed to be open source, allowing researchers, developers, and environmental stakeholders to explore, improve, and reuse its tools and methodology.

Expected Impact

Active Fire Calendar aims to make long-term satellite fire information more accessible and understandable, particularly for regions where environmental monitoring resources are limited.

By providing a harmonized historical perspective and an accessible visualization tool, the project seeks to support scientific research, improve awareness of seasonal fire patterns, and contribute to more informed environmental management in Haut-Katanga and potentially other regions.

Source: NASA Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS).
